about: LINDISFARENA (Lindisfarne), 793-1066: Saint Cuthbert's island thirteen days after the heathen men, and what becomes of it. One port. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/lindisfarena.md and the spine; a draft for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not checked; 'invented' marks what the sources do not give. Woven with the region on 7 Oct 2026: ties to Bebbanburg, Gyrwe and Hi pointed at real people and made to run both ways, beats pointed at their cards (Data/encounters/northumbria_irish_sea_793.json).

ports.summary: A bishop's monastery on a low island that the sea cuts off twice a day, the shrine of Saint Cuthbert, with the kings' rock of Bebbanburg in plain sight to the south. On 21 June 793 it is thirteen days since heathen men came from the north: the doors are off the church, some brethren are dead, some drowned, and boys of the house are gone in the ships. Nothing is sold here by custom. This is a house that receives: a merchant comes with wine, wax, oil, lead and grain, and leaves with thanks, letters, a little silver and the bishop's list.
ports.seasons: The tide is the clock: the sand to the mainland is dry twice a day and drowned twice. Saint Cuthbert's day is the twentieth of March and falls in Lent, when a brother keeps the fast alone on the rock offshore; the gathering is at Saint Aidan's mass at the end of August. Seals pup on the sands at the back end of the year, geese come with the first frosts, and from the first of May to the end of September every brother looks north before he looks anywhere else.

history.text: About this year Aidan comes from Hi at King Oswald's asking and is given the island for his bishop's seat.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.3; en.wikipedia Lindisfarne

history.text: Bishop Finan (651 to 661) builds a church not of stone but of hewn oak, thatched with reeds. Bishop Eadberht (688 to 698) takes off the thatch and covers roof and walls with plates of lead.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.25

history.text: Cuthbert dies on Farne on the twentieth of March. A brother on a height on the island waits for two candles shown from the rock; the body comes over by ship and is buried in a stone coffin at the right side of the altar.
history.source: Bede, Life of Saint Cuthbert 40 (tr. Giles)

history.text: The grave is opened after eleven years and the body found whole. It is laid in a new coffin of carved oak above the floor of the sanctuary; Bishop Eadberht dies soon after and is laid in the grave beneath.
history.source: Bede, Life of Saint Cuthbert 42-43; Ecclesiastical History IV.30

history.text: Between about this year and 720 a great gospel book is written on the island on some hundred and fifty calfskins. The house that made it has not been found by the diggers.
history.source: en.wikipedia Lindisfarne Gospels; Design/content/lore/texts_books.md (?)

history.text: King Ceolwulf gives up his kingdom and enters the house as a monk. From then the brethren may drink wine or ale, who before had only milk or water.
history.source: Symeon of Durham, History of the Kings, s.a. 854 (tr. Stevenson 1855)

history.text: About this year Offa, son of King Aldfrith, flees to Saint Cuthbert's body and is dragged away from it almost dead of hunger. King Eadberht shuts Bishop Cynewulf up at Bebbanburg.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 750; History of the Church of Durham xvii (Stevenson 1855)

history.text: Higbald takes the bishop's seat. He holds it until his death on 25 May 803.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xix-xx; en.wikipedia Higbald of Lindisfarne

history.text: On 23 April the body of Sicga, the ealdorman who killed King Ælfwald and died by his own hand, is carried to the island. The same year: lights and whirlwinds, fiery dragons in the sky, and a great famine.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 793; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 793 (Giles 1847; texts_793.json chronicle_793)

history.text: On 8 June heathen men come from the north in ships. Some of the brethren they kill, some they carry off in chains, most they strip and drive out of doors, and some they drown in the sea. The bishop's seat stays where it is.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xx (Stevenson 1855); Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 793; chronicle_793.json 793-06-08-lindisfarena-raid

history.text: Later in the year Alcuin writes from Francia to Higbald and the brethren. He promises that when King Charles comes home he will go to him and do what he can for the youths led away captive.
history.source: Alcuin to Higbald, MGH Epistolae IV no. 20; chronicle_793.json 793-autumn-alcuin-captives

history.text: Heathen men plunder the monastery at the mouth of the Tyne. Their leader is killed and a storm breaks their ships.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xx; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 794

history.text: In May Osbald, king for twenty-seven days, flees to the island and goes from it by ship with some of the brethren to the king of the Picts. He dies an abbot in 799.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 796; chronicle_793.json 796-05-osbald-flees

history.text: On Christmas eve a great wind; the sea comes over its bounds and floods the land.
history.source: chronicle_793.json (Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 800)

history.text: Higbald dies on 25 May. Ecgberht is hallowed bishop at Bywell on 11 June.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xx; chronicle_793.json 803-05-25-higbald

history.text: Ecgred is bishop (830 to 845), a man of noble birth and energetic. He builds a church at Norham on the Tweed and moves King Ceolwulf's body there; one later book says Saint Cuthbert's body went with it for a time.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xx; Historia de Sancto Cuthberto as reported by en.wikipedia (?)

history.text: About this year a book of the names of the house's friends, living and dead, is begun in gold and silver letters, probably here.
history.source: en.wikipedia Durham Liber Vitae (?)

history.text: The heathen army holds York. On 21 March both Northumbrian kings, Osberht and Ælle, are killed there. The army comes no further north than the Tyne.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xxi; chronicle_793.json

history.text: Halfdan winters on the Tyne. Bishop Eardulf and Abbot Eadred leave the island with Saint Cuthbert's body, Saint Oswald's head, some of Aidan's bones and the bones of three bishops, two hundred and forty-one years after the founding.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xxi (Stevenson 1855)

history.text: After seven years on the road the body rests at Chester-le-Street. King Guthred's law gives thirty-seven days' peace to anyone who flees to it.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 883

history.text: Between 883 and 895 Scots cross the Tweed and plunder the monastery of Lindisfarne.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xxviii (the year within that span is not given)

history.text: The men of York ravage the island of Lindisfarne and kill many.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 941 (Stevenson 1855)

history.text: Bishop Aldhun carries the body from Chester-le-Street to Durham. The island is from now a holy place of Durham's saint and not his house.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 995; History of the Church of Durham xxxvi

history.text: Malcolm, king of Scots, harries Northumbria and breaks the peace of Saint Cuthbert on the island.
history.source: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 1061

eras.text: The wound. Bishop Higbald counts what is gone and will not leave. The church has no doors and half its lamps; the cross in the graveyard has lost its head; the writing house has been turned out on its floor. Famine is in the land in 793, so grain is worth more here than silver. The house takes wine, wax, oil, lead and bread corn, and pays in what it has: a little old silver, wool, a letter, a prayer by name. In 796 a king of twenty-seven days comes over the sand in a hurry.

Mended. Bishop Ecgberht, then Heathwred. The doors hang, the head of the cross is run on again with lead, new boys are in the school. The sea broke over the low ground at Christmas 800 and the brethren still talk of it. The scribes work again and want calfskin and colours. Styca coins of the Northumbrian kings pass at the cellarer's door, small and getting baser.

Half a house. Bishop Ecgred builds at Norham on the Tweed, and the bishops are as often there as here; the island keeps the shrine, the graveyard, the school and a farm on the north shore that turns calves into pages. About 840 the book of names is begun. Pennies of Wessex turn up beside the brass stycas. After 867 York is the army's, and the talk at the guest fire is of how far the Tyne is.

The leaving. In 875 the bishop and the saint's people go over the sand with the coffin on a cart and do not come back for a lifetime. A few stay: a priest, the farm, the fishers. The church is locked and the shrine is an empty place on the floor that people still kneel beside.

A cell and a farm under the bishop at Chester-le-Street. Graves are still dug and stones still carved. No one guards it: Scots plunder it in the time of King Guthred, and in 941 the men of York come and kill many. A merchant finds a priest, a few households, sheep, seals and a very good anchorage with nobody to take a toll.

Durham's island. The body lies at Durham from 995 and the island is where it began: pilgrims cross the sand barefoot at the ebb, a priest keeps the old church, and a penny of King Edward is lost in the grass. In 1061 the king of Scots breaks the saint's peace here. The land is the earls' of Bebbanburg in all but name.

sites.name: The Ouse
sites.see: A pool of quiet water inside the sands, with a shelving beach of shingle and black weed. In front, two small tarred boats drawn up and the marks of many keels, some of them long; behind, the ridge of the Heugh and the lead roof of the church catching the light. Terns, the slap of the tide coming in over the flats, a smell of weed and wet wool.
sites.source: The harbour pool is calm in westerlies (Research/water_levels/north_and_norway.md); where boats lay is not recorded. In 687 Cuthbert's body came from Farne by ship (Bede, Life of Cuthbert 40). The keel marks of June 793 are the game's.

sites.name: The pilgrims' sand
sites.see: Three quarters of a mile of wet sand between the island and the mainland, shining like a shield at the ebb and gone altogether at the flood. A line of footprints and cart ruts runs across it, already filling. Far out a man leads an ox cart, small as a beetle; behind him the hills of the mainland, and the sea coming round both ends at once without any noise.
sites.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.3: twice a day enclosed by the sea like an island, twice joined to the land. No causeway before modern times; crossed on foot or by cart at low water (dossier, section 1).

sites.name: Saint Peter's church
sites.see: A long low church of hewn oak, sheathed roof and walls in grey lead so that it looks cast in one piece. In 793 the doorway stands open with the hinges torn out and daylight falls on a swept floor; inside, to the right of the altar, the carved oak coffin of Saint Cuthbert stands above the ground, untouched. Few lamps. The brethren sing the hours with gaps where voices used to be.
sites.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.25 (oak, then lead plates); Life of Cuthbert 42-43 (the coffin above the floor). The doors off: the spine's picture of Higbald; the body was not taken (spine, holy_island). Sanctuary at the body: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 750.

sites.name: The graveyard and Bishop Æthelwold's cross
sites.see: Low mounds in rows, feet to the sea, each with a scatter of white pebbles from the shore laid on it, and here and there a small carved stone, painted, with a name and a cross. In the middle a tall stone cross with the bishop's name cut on it: in 793 its head lies in the grass beside it in pieces. New graves at the near end, the turf still cut square.
sites.source: DigVentures and Durham University, burials of the 7th to 11th centuries: shrouded, feet to the sea, white quartz pebbles on the graves; the name stones (English Heritage collection). Æthelwold's cross, broken by the heathen in 793 and run together with lead: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xii. King Oswald's head lay in this graveyard (Bede III.12).

sites.name: The pit of the washing water
sites.see: South of the church, a square pit lined with wood and filled to the top with small stones, no bigger than a hearth. A woman kneels and takes a pinch of the earth beside it into a twist of cloth. The lead wall of the church behind, a lark going up, the sound of the brethren through the wall.
sites.source: Bede, Life of Saint Cuthbert 41: the water that washed the body was poured into a pit on the south side of the church, wood-lined and filled with small stones, and earth from it healed a boy.

sites.name: The writing house
sites.see: A plain timber room with its shutters wide for the light. Slanted desks, horns of ink, a stretched calfskin drying on a frame by the door. In 793 the book chest stands with its lid split and a brother is sorting loose leaves into piles on the floor, some trodden, one with a boot print across a line of English verse. The smell is of skin, gall and lamp smoke.
sites.source: The writing room has not been found (dossier, section 2); that books were made here is the Lindisfarne Gospels. The riddle leaf: riddles_793.json riddle_exeter_01_storm_land, bought here 793 to 875 (set exeter_storm). The plundered chest is the spine's (riddle_road hook).

sites.name: The cellarer's door
sites.see: A thatched store with a half door and a beam scale hanging in the opening. Inside, in the dark, casks on their sides, cakes of wax under a cloth, sacks of barley counted and counted again. A brother with keys at his belt stands in the doorway with a tally stick; behind him a boy is sweeping up spilled corn grain by grain.
sites.source: No market, toll or fair is recorded: the house receives (dossier, section 4). What it took in: wine (Symeon s.a. 854), lead (Bede III.25), wax, oil and incense as any church. The cellarer is the Rule's officer; the door is the game's.

sites.name: The guest house
sites.see: A long hut outside the boundary ditch with a fire down the middle and benches along the walls. A carter, two pilgrims with their feet in a tub and a king's man who says nothing share one pot. On a board by the fire a game is half played with pieces of bone and one of blue glass with a white crown. Smoke, wet leather, barley broth.
sites.source: No guest house has been found (dossier, section 2): every house under a rule kept one (?). The blue glass gaming king of 700 to 900, like pieces from Dorestad and Dublin: DigVentures 2020. The boundary ditch: DigVentures 2025.

sites.name: The smith's shed
sites.see: An open shed downwind of everything else: a clay hearth, a stone anvil, a small domed oven with green glass run down its lip. Slag underfoot and bright beads of spilled copper. In 793 the smith is not making anything fine. He is drawing nails for doors and melting lead in an iron ladle.
sites.source: An oven for copper or glass and a smithy with slag and copper droplets, with six coins of about 840 beside it: en.wikipedia Lindisfarne; DigVentures 2020.

sites.name: The watch on the Heugh
sites.see: A bare ridge of black rock along the island's south edge. On its top a small stone chapel and beside it the footing of something taller. From here everything shows: the Ouse below, the crag of Beblowe to the east with nothing on it, the Farne rocks, the kings' fort on its rock to the south, and to the north only sea. A brother sits with his back to the wall and his face to the north.
sites.source: In 687 a brother waited on a height for two candles shown from Farne (Bede, Life of Cuthbert 40). Footings of a small stone church and a tower-like building on the Heugh, dug 2016-17 (dossier, from memory) (?). No beacon or daymark before 1810; no castle on Beblowe before 1550.

sites.name: Saint Cuthbert's rock
sites.see: A hump of black stone a bowshot off the shore, with turf on top and a low wall of piled stones. At the ebb a man can walk to it over weed and pools; at the flood it is its own island. Eider ducks sit on the water round it. In Lent there is one brother on it and a thread of smoke.
sites.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History IV.30: Cuthbert and after him Eadberht kept Lent alone on a place surrounded by the sea at the flood. Wall footings show in the turf today (English Heritage). The eiders are there; the story that Cuthbert protected them has no early evidence (dossier, section 8).

sites.name: The cattle steading on the north shore
sites.see: Beyond the dunes, where the island is all sand, grass and wind: low buildings with stone feet and turf roofs, a yard of trodden mud, small black cattle with their calves kept close. Calfskins are pegged out on the grass, hair side down, and a herdsman scrapes one with a curved knife. Surf on the north beach, and the smell of the dung heap and the lime pit.
sites.source: Green Shiel: five stone-footed buildings of the 9th century, whose cattle bones may mean calfskin for the writing room (en.wikipedia Lindisfarne; English Heritage research). A farm there before 800 is likely but not shown (?).

people.name: Higbald
people.trait: The bishop who was there on 8 June 793 and stayed: counts what is gone, writes to Alcuin, keeps the brethren on the island.
people.want: The youths found and bought back; the shrine made whole; wax and wine for the altar.
people.fear: A second sail; the brethren asking to leave the island.
people.voice: Tired and exact; lists what is missing on his fingers.
people.looks: Past sixty, gaunt, tonsured white, a patched habit of undyed wool and a plain wooden staff since the good one was taken; behind him a church with its doors off.
knows: the names of the boys who were carried off, their kin, and what the house can pay for each
what was taken by weight: the silver from the altar, the cover of a gospel book, the good staff
what Alcuin writes from King Charles's court, and that the king has been asked about the captives
which king sits at Bebbanburg this season and how little that helped
who has taken sanctuary at the saint's body and what came of it

ties.note: the same person
Alcuin's letters of 793 are to him; he answers by any ship that will take a letter south
his own oblate, one of the youths carried off
knows the brothers' family and sends the elder word
the monk who brings him Alcuin's answers
the abbot of Hi, the mother house; they pray for each other's dead
the cellarer serves him, and tells him each week what there is not
the thegn of the rock's gate saw the sails and could not come; the bishop has never said a word of blame, and takes the two wardens he sends each new moon without comment
the fisherman under the rock rows his messages when the flats are covered, and is paid in blessings and the house's old nets
the steward of the rock sends fish and butter over the flats since the raid, and has never put it on a tally
his priest on the rock, schooled on the island, who crosses the flats to him at each new moon with the hall's news
a monk of Tallaght in Ireland, by letter only, who prays for the daughter house's dead and wants its saints' days
the new archbishop keeps more spears than books; the bishop answers York's letters carefully and at length
the abbot of Bede's house sent bread and two brothers north in the week after the raid; the houses pray for each other's dead
the abbess of Hild's house, whose dead his own house prays for; she asks his counsel about moving the saints
his kinsman's widow, who lives by the ditch with her household, and is the one person on the island who argues with him
the scribe who writes his letters and keeps the list of what is gone
the house's boatman, as his father was: the only man on the island who gives the bishop orders, twice a day

lines.greet: You came in on the same beach they did. Forgive the brothers for watching you. Sit. What do you carry, and where do you go after this?
lines.greet_again: The boat I know. Good. I have kept count since you left: nothing more is gone, and nothing has come back.
rumour: They took boys. Not for killing. A boy who can write is worth more to them alive, God help him, and that is my one hope.
Alcuin writes that our sins brought this. Perhaps. I notice the letter came by a ship, and the ship had to be paid.
The king's hall can see this church from its wall. I am told the wind was wrong for them that day.
Brothers ask me whether the saint was asleep. I tell them he is where he was. It is we who were moved.
lines.saying: Count what is lost once, aloud, and write it down. After that, count what is left.
lines.farewell: Go on the ebb, and God keep your boat. If you see an English boy in the north, ask him his name before you ask his price.

people.source: Alcuin to Higbald, 793 (MGH Epistolae IV no. 20); Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xix-xx; en.wikipedia Higbald of Lindisfarne (bishop 780/781, died 25 May 803); spine cast.higbald. His birth year is a guess (?). The lines are the game's.

people.name: Tidwine
people.trait: An oblate of twelve who could write a fair hand: sold north, he lives by being useful and forgets his English a word at a time.
people.want: At first, home. Later, he is not sure: he has a place, a skill and perhaps a wife among the heathen.
people.voice: As a boy, whispers; as a man, speaks Norse with an English turn and Latin only in his sleep.
people.looks: As a boy: small, cropped hair, a torn habit, bare feet, a thrall's collar of rope. As a man of forty: a trader's servant in northern dress who still holds a stick like a pen.
knows: he is not on the island on 21 June 793: he is met in the north, and here only if he is brought home
which ship took him and where each of the others was sold, as far as he saw
how silver is weighed and tallied in a northern hall
the psalms by heart, in a hand and a voice that have not been used for years

ties.note: the same person
his elder brother, who sails with the merchant to find him
the bishop's own oblate
the scribe set him his first letters and kept his practice leaf
taken on Thorleif's ship (?)
bought for his tallying and kept
the thegn of the gate who taught his brother the spear; for one whole winter in the north he told himself the rock would send a ship
the old master at Gyrwe, who taught his brother and knew him as a small boy before he went to the island
the thegn's widow whose nephew Wigfrith shared his bench in the school; she asks after both of them by name

lines.greet: I know the bell. I had forgotten I knew it. Do not tell them yet that I am slow with the words.
lines.greet_again: You. They have given me the tally of the wax. It is the same work as in the north, only the wax is for God.
rumour: Brother Ceolhelm kept my leaf. Seven lines of the same letter, all bad. He showed it to me and neither of us could speak.
They were not cruel to me, mostly. That is the part nobody here wants to hear.
I dream in their speech. The psalms come out right in the morning, so I say nothing.
lines.saying: A thing is worth what a man will weigh out for it. I learned that as the thing.
lines.farewell: Go safely. If you pass the hall where I was, tell the woman there the boy is well. She will know which.

people.source: invented: one of the youths of Lindisfarne whom Alcuin hoped to ransom (letter to Higbald, 793); spine cast.tidwine. Christian captives were at Birka in 829 (Rimbert c. 11).

people.name: Hunfrith
people.trait: Cellarer and keeper of the guest house: a broad practical man who hid under an upturned boat on the eighth of June and has told nobody.
people.want: Full casks, bread corn through the famine, and a merchant who comes back when he says he will.
people.fear: That somebody saw him go under the boat. And an empty store at the start of Lent.
people.voice: Brisk and kindly; says what a thing weighs before he says what it is. Laughs at his own stomach.
people.looks: About forty, stout for a hungry year, a ring of red hair round a sunburned tonsure, an undyed wool habit kilted up, a bunch of iron keys and a notched tally stick at his belt.
knows: what the house will take and what it gives for it: wine, wax, oil, lead, incense, bread corn
who is in the guest house tonight and what road they came by
the tide for the sand today, to the width of a hand
which of the house's farms on the mainland have corn and which sent excuses
every merchant who has called since he took the keys, and what each one promised

ties.note: holds the keys for him
the boatman brings his casks over; they have quarrelled every week for fifteen years
she fed the brethren from her own store the week after the raid, and he has not yet paid it back
the scribe wants calfskin and colours; the cellarer wants bread, and the purse is one purse
keeps the bed nearest the fire for the letter carrier, who feels the cold
the two houses lend each other wine in a bad year and count it carefully (?)
the guest-master of the mother house, whom he has never met: fifteen years of messages by ship, mostly about wine
the cellarer on the cliff: ten years of letters about the price of wax, and not one of them agreed
the letter carrier from York, who has the bed nearest the fire and still complains of the cold

lines.greet: A keel with casks in her. Come to the half door, friend. I will tell you now we pay badly and pray well.
lines.greet_again: There you are. I told the brothers you would come back and they said merchants never do. I had a loaf on it.
rumour: They drank the altar wine on the beach and left the cask. A good cask. I use it. I do not tell the bishop which one it is.
A king's man has slept three nights by my fire and asked nothing. In my trade that is a man who is counting.
Corn from our own farm at Norham came short again. The reeve there says famine. His horse is fat.
lines.saying: We owe King Ceolwulf our ale. He gave up a kingdom, and we gave up water.
lines.farewell: The sand is good until the weed on the far post is wet. After that you swim or you stay to supper.

people.source: invented; the office is the Rule's. Wine and ale since King Ceolwulf, 737: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 854. The estate at Norham: the same, though the church there is Ecgred's, after 830 (?). Name: Hun- + -frith.

people.name: Ceolhelm
people.trait: Master of the writing house: thin-skinned, exact, and angrier about a trodden leaf than about his own split lip.
people.want: The scattered leaves found, the book chest filled again, and calfskin, orpiment and red lead to do it with.
people.fear: That he will die with the quires unbound and a boy who cannot rule a line.
people.voice: Precise, and bitter in a small way, like a note in a margin. Corrects your word, then answers the question.
people.looks: Early thirties, narrow, pale, a healing cut through the lip, tonsured, ink to the second knuckle of the right hand; a penknife on a thong and a leaf of practice letters folded in his sleeve.
knows: what a book is worth and to whom: the skins, the year of a scribe's life, the cover, and what a heathen sees in it
which leaves are missing from which book, to the line
the English riddle verses the house had in one quire, and which leaf of it is still here
what is in the libraries at Gyrwe and York, and what they lack
how to read a rune-cut name and a Roman one: the stones in the graveyard have both

ties.note: set the boy his letters; keeps his practice leaf in his sleeve
writes the bishop's letters and the list of what is gone
skins or bread: the argument is twenty years old
knew him as a schoolboy at Gyrwe and thinks leaving the cloister a waste of a good hand
they trade lists of books each other's house lacks
heard Alcuin teach at York for one winter and has quoted him ever since
writes to the house on the cliff for the loan of exemplars (?)
the scribe at York has the better library and the worse hand; both know it, and neither will write it down
Torhtred of Bede's house was on the island for an exemplar in June 793; Ceolhelm has wondered ever since what left in his shirt
the second hand in the mother house's writing room: they lend each other exemplars, and blame each other for the errors
a priest on the Dee he has never seen, to whom he once sent a quill and a recipe for ink

lines.greet: Mind the floor. Every one of those piles is a book, or was. Do you read? No matter. Do you carry skins?
lines.greet_again: The merchant. Good. I have a list for you, shorter than the last, because I have given up hoping for the blue.
rumour: They tore the cover off and left the gospel in the nettles. A year of my master's life, and they wanted the lid.
One quire of English verse went three ways. I have a leaf. The wind had the rest, or someone's shirt did.
A book is a herd of calves and a year. Tell a heathen that and he will sell it back by the calf.
lines.saying: Three fingers hold the pen and the whole back aches. You may write that in the margin; everybody does.
lines.farewell: Keep the leaf dry and flat, and away from your Northman's fingers. Go with God. Bring calfskin.

people.source: invented; the house made the Lindisfarne Gospels about 715 to 720 (some 150 skins). The riddle leaf is riddles_793.json riddle_exeter_01_storm_land. The scribe's complaint is the common colophon of early scribes, in our own words. Name: Ceol- + -helm.

people.name: Eadstan
people.trait: The house's boatman and the man who knows the sand: a layman, weathered, short with fools, who pulled two brothers out of the sea in June and could not reach a third.
people.want: A second pair of hands he can trust in the boat, and somebody to learn the marks before he dies.
people.fear: Fog on the flats with a cart half way over.
people.voice: Says a thing once, in as few words as it takes. Speaks of the tide as 'she'.
people.looks: Near fifty, short and wide, a face like a dried apple, grey hair tied back with a thong, a sealskin jerkin over a wool shirt, bare legs, a sounding pole taller than himself.
knows: the hours the sand is dry today and tomorrow, and where it is quick
the way into the Ouse and the reefs to the east and north of the island
the Farne rocks: which have water, which have seals, which will take a boat in a north-easter
what the long ships looked like and which way they went: north, close in
who fishes where from the Tweed to the Coquet

ties.note: ferries his casks and argues about every one
the bishop's boatman, as his father was
his wife's sister married into her household
the fisherman under the rock sets his nets on Eadstan's marks, and says the saint's ducks told him where
one steersman knows another; they compare sands, his and the Frisian's
lies at the guest house on the Tyne when he goes for casks; the guest-master asks forty questions and gets four answers
the boatman under Hild's cliff: they have sheltered in each other's water, and each owes the other a boat hook

lines.greet: You came in on the last of the flood. Lucky or taught? Pull her up past the weed line. She comes higher than you think.
lines.greet_again: Same boat, same place on the shingle. You listen. Most do not, and I get their anchors.
rumour: Long ships, low, more oars than I could count. They went north with the land close on the left hand. Men who knew the coast.
I got two brothers out by the hair. The third had his habit on, and wet wool is an anchor.
Seals are early on the far sand. My father said that means a hard back end. He said it most years.
lines.saying: She waits for no bishop. Twice a day he is my better and twice a day I am his.
lines.farewell: Out by the south, keep the black rock open of the point. If you see fog, you have not left yet.

people.source: invented; lay people lived on the island (men, women and children in the graveyard: DigVentures). 'Some they drowned in the sea': Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xx. The tide: Bede III.3. Name: Ead- + -stan.

people.name: Æthelgyth
people.trait: A thegn's widow who gave her land to the saint and lives by the ditch with her household: her sister's son Wigfrith was one of the boys taken.
people.want: Wigfrith back, or word of him, or failing both a stone with his name on it.
people.fear: That the bishop will spend what silver is left on a book cover and not on a boy.
people.voice: Courteous and unhurried, used to being obeyed. Asks a hard question as if it were about the weather.
people.looks: Past forty, upright, a linen head-cloth with a narrow band of gold thread at the brow, a dark blue gown pinned with two small silver pins, a bone comb and a key hanging from her girdle.
knows: the family of every boy who was taken, and what each could raise toward a ransom
who lies where in the graveyard and whose stone is whose
what the king's thegns say of the raid in their own halls, which is not what they say here
the worth of wool, cloth and stock between the Tweed and the Aln

ties.note: her husband's kinsman; she is the one person on the island who argues with him
he owes her a week of bread from June 793; she will not let him pay
her nephew's bench-fellow in the school; she asks after both by name
by marriage, through her household
a cousin of her husband's house at York; she can speak for a merchant to him, or against
the thegn who held the rock's gate on the eighth of June is her dead husband's brother, and she has not spoken to him since (?)
the old ale-wife of the vill under the rock; they send each other malt and the names of the hungry over the flats
the host on the strand at York lodges her messengers, and sends back the price of wool with them

lines.greet: You are the Frisian's boat. Come and sit; you will be asked for nothing in this house but news. Which ports do you make this year?
lines.greet_again: Welcome back. I looked for your sail at each feast. Tell me first whether you have been north. Then eat.
rumour: My husband's brother stood on the rock and watched the smoke. He says they had no ships ready. They had horses.
The bishop grieves for his book cover. I do not blame him. I only ask him which of the two can be frightened.
Three families have sold cattle toward the ransom. Nobody knows yet whom to pay.
lines.saying: A friend is good far or near, and better near. Mine are far, so I feed merchants.
lines.farewell: God go with you. If the boy is dead, tell me straight, at this door, before you tell anyone else.

people.source: invented; from the woman of rank buried here in the 9th century with gold thread at her head and children round her, and the bone comb (DigVentures 2024, 2025, 2026). The proverb is the Durham Proverbs' 'Freond deah feor ge neah: byth near nyttra', our rendering. The nephew Wigfrith is invented. Name: Æthel- + -gyth.

people.name: Eardulf
people.trait: The last bishop on the island: patient, stubborn, a man who decides slowly and then does not look back.
people.want: The saint's body and the saint's people kept together, wherever that has to be.
people.fear: Halfdan's army on the Tyne, two days' march off; and leading his people the wrong way.
people.voice: Quiet and plain, with long silences he does not fill. Asks how many days, how many carts, how much bread.
people.looks: About fifty in 875, heavy-shouldered, grey tonsure, a travelling cloak over the habit and stout shoes; a plain staff, and the look of a man who has already packed.
knows: where the heathen army lies and which way it is likely to turn
which of the saint's estates still pay and which are burned
what must be carried when a house leaves: the body, Oswald's head, Aidan's bones, the books, the head of the cross
the peace a man has at the saint's body, and what it costs to break it

ties.note: the abbot of the mother house is sending its own treasures to Ireland, and writes to him how it is done (?)
his archbishop sits in a city the army holds (?)
the priest who keeps Bede's house on the Tyne is nearer the army than he is; his news is the bishop's warning (?)
the reeve of the rock would rather the saint's lands had a lay protector, and has offered himself (?)
an old cliff man of Hild's emptied house sent to ask where its people should go; he had no answer then, and has one now (?)

lines.greet: A merchant, this year of all years. You are welcome. Tell me what you saw at the Tyne mouth, slowly, and leave nothing out.
lines.greet_again: You again, and still afloat. Then God has not given up on trade. Sit down. I have a use for a keel.
rumour: Abbot Eadred came over the hills from Luel to tell me to go. A man does not walk that far to say a thing he doubts.
Seven of the young men carry the coffin and let no other hand touch it. They have already quarrelled about the order.
My predecessors lie under this floor. Three of them are coming with us in a box. The rest must keep the house.
lines.saying: The island is where he was. The saint is where his people are.
lines.farewell: Go while the sand is dry. If we meet again it will be on a road, and I will remember the boat.

people.source: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xxi, xxvi-xxvii (Stevenson 1855): Eardulf and Eadred, abbot of Carlisle, left in 875 with the body; seven bearers, four named (Hunred, Stitheard, Edmund, Franco). Bishop 854 to 899: en.wikipedia Eardulf of Lindisfarne. His birth year is a guess (?). The lines are the game's.

people.name: Leofstan
people.trait: The priest Durham keeps on the island: cheerful, lonely, and prouder of the place than of himself.
people.want: Pilgrims, and a roof on the old church that keeps the rain off them.
people.fear: The Scots from over the Tweed. The peace of the saint is a strong wall until somebody walks through it.
people.voice: Talks a great deal, having few to talk to. Tells the old stories as if he had been there, and says so.
people.looks: About forty, small and wind-reddened, a fringe of sandy hair, a much-mended black gown hitched up for walking the sand, a wooden cross on a cord and a pilgrim's staff he lends out.
knows: every story of the saint and which stone each one happened at
the crossing hours, which he calls from the shore for strangers
what Durham's clerks want fetched and carried, and what the earl's men at Bebbanburg are saying
where the old house stood: the pit, the cross socket, the ditch, the rock

ties.note: the earl's reeve grazes sheep on what the priest calls the saint's grass (?)
through his bishop at Durham, who answers to York (?)
says the king walked barefoot to the saint's body at Durham and gave land; he was a boy and did not see it (?)
a widow of York who keeps the old ale-house: he lodges with her when he carries letters to the archbishop, and brings her the island's news
the earl's reeve under the cliff at Whitby sends fish in Lent, and gets prayers and gossip back

lines.greet: A boat in the Ouse! We get three a year. Come up, come up. Have you seen the pit? I will show you the pit.
lines.greet_again: I knew the sail. I said to the sheep, that is my merchant. Come and tell me what year it is in the world.
rumour: The heathen came in on that very beach. My house has told it for two hundred and fifty years and it has lost nothing in the telling.
A man dug here for the old bishops' silver. He found a comb with half a name on it. It served him right.
The king of Scots was here with his men. He prayed first. Then he took the cattle.
lines.saying: The saint went to Durham for the walls. He left me the view.
lines.farewell: Cross with the ebb, and give my greeting to anywhere with more than six people in it.

people.source: invented; the island after 995 was Durham's (dossier, section 5), with carved stones to the late 10th century and a penny of Edward the Confessor of 1046-48 found. Malcolm in 1061: Symeon, History of the Kings. Cnut's barefoot walk to Durham is Symeon's (History of the Church of Durham, from memory) (?). Name: Leof- + -stan.

stories.title: The bishop's count
stories.summary: Higbald has a list: the names of the boys, the silver from the altar by weight, the cover of a gospel book. He gives it to a merchant who goes north, with what the house can pay and a letter for Alcuin. What comes back down the coast, and in what state, is the merchant's doing.
stories.picture: A gaunt old bishop in a doorless church doorway at low sun, holding up one hand with three fingers counted off, a scribe behind him writing on a wax tablet, the sea grey beyond.

beats.text: Higbald counts on his fingers: Tidwine, Wigfrith, Hereric and the rest; so many pounds of altar silver; one book cover of gold and stones. He will pay in wax, wine or what silver is left, and he hands over a letter for Alcuin. (Sets lf_knows_boys.)
Æthelgyth stops the merchant by the broken cross. Three families have sold cattle. She names what each can add, and asks to be told before the bishop if the news is bad.
Sigewine waits at Alcuin's hospice with the answer and a small bag of the king's alms for the ransom (?). He needs a ship that goes north, and he is sick on all of them.
Church things sold as curios, and a dealer who bought three English boys in the autumn of 793. He remembers the one who could count. (Sets lf_trail_north.)
Thorleif's hall: a brooch on a woman's breast that was the corner of a book, two English boys with the swine, and a price in silver by weight or a sword. Prayers buy nothing. (Sets lf_boy_found.)
The boat comes into the Ouse with one more aboard than she left with, or with a small heavy thing in a cloth. Eadstan sees who is in the bow before anyone, and for once runs.
At York the letter carrier Sigewine has the same names by heart and eleven pounds collected, and wants a keel that goes north of the Tyne and comes back.
The thegn who had the watch on the rock hears the names, takes off his arm ring, and asks that it be carried north toward any one of them.
The second copy of the list goes to the mother house in the west, where the names are read at the altar and a man of the outer islands says which way the ships went home.

endings.how: You found Tidwine, paid for him and brought him over the sand while Higbald lived.
endings.text: The bishop says the boy's name once and then cannot say anything. Ceolhelm takes a folded leaf out of his sleeve. Tidwine is given the tally of the wax, because he will not go near the writing house for a year.
endings.reward: The ransom the house promised, in silver, wax and wool to about 300 d; Higbald, Æthelgyth and Hunfrith as fast friends; Beornwine's loyalty for life; free lodging and stores at the guest house for this merchant and his heir; a mass said by name each year.

endings.how: You brought him home after May 803, to Bishop Ecgberht and a house that had given him up.
endings.text: Nobody at the gate knows the man in northern dress until he sings the response at vespers from the back. Higbald is under the floor. Æthelgyth has kept the bench.
endings.reward: Half the silver, since the purse was spent on doors and lead; the same friends, less one; a name stone cut for the merchant's own dead at the house's cost.

endings.how: You found him and he would not come: he has a place there. You carried back his words and a leaf in his hand.
endings.text: Higbald reads the leaf twice and says the letters have got worse. He has it sewn into the book of the house. Beornwine does not speak for three days and then asks to go north again, to visit.
endings.reward: No ransom spent: the bishop gives a third of it for the news. A standing welcome at Tidwine's hall in the north (a friend in a heathen port); Æthelgyth's friendship if Wigfrith's fate was told to her first.

endings.how: You bought back the mount that had been made a brooch, and no boy.
endings.text: Ceolhelm weeps over a thumb's length of gold. Æthelgyth looks at it, and at the merchant, and goes back to her house without a word.
endings.reward: Its weight in silver twice over from the bishop (about 120 d) and the scribe as a fast friend; Æthelgyth cool from that day, and her door at York with her.

endings.how: Higbald died, the years ran out, and nothing came back.
endings.text: The list is copied into the book of the house under the year. The names of the boys are read once a year on the eighth of June for as long as there are brethren on the island.
endings.reward: Nothing but the list itself (a text for the chest), and the right to hear the names read.

stories.reward: A bishop's house that knows the merchant by his boat for two generations, the ransom in goods and silver, and a friend at one end or the other of the northern road.

stories.title: The leaf that asks who drives it
stories.summary: One quire of English riddles was scattered when the writing house was turned out: a leaf is still here, a second went to Gyrwe in a brother's shirt, and the third is in a sea chest that has not come ashore yet. Each asks who sends the storm. Read together they name a landing among the rocks off Bebbanburg that no other ship uses.
stories.picture: A single trodden parchment leaf on a desk under an open shutter, a boot print across its lines of verse, a thin ink-stained hand holding it flat, and through the window grey rocks far out at sea.

beats.text: Ceolhelm sells a fair copy of his leaf for ten pennies, grudging every one: the storm that walks the land and burns the halls. He will not give the answer. He says the other two leaves would. (Gives riddle_exeter_01_storm_land.)
A brother at Bede's house has the second leaf, the storm under the sea, and knows very well where it came from. He will sell a copy too, and asks whether Ceolhelm is still angry.
After the wrecking storms of 799 a sea chest lies above the tide line under the cliff. In it, dry in a waxed cloth, the third leaf: the storm in the sky.

With all three leaves, Eadstan is asked what rock 'holds its breath under the north-east wind'. He looks at the merchant for a long time, then points with his pole at the Farne rocks and says which, and how to come at it.
Among the islands off the kings' rock: a gut between two skerries with deep water, a shingle bed and no swell in a north-easter. Nobody is there to take a toll.

endings.how: You gathered and solved all three leaves and kept the landing to yourself.
endings.text: The house has a harbour of its own on the Northumbrian coast, known to one steersman and passed to the heir with the chest.
endings.reward: rw_cove_farne: a sheltered landing among the Farne islands, safe in a north-easterly gale and free of toll, for the house only.

endings.how: You brought copies of all three leaves back to Ceolhelm, so that the quire could be written out again.
endings.text: He rules the lines himself and has it bound with the first boards the house has had since June. In the margin of the last leaf he writes a short line about a merchant, not wholly rude.
endings.reward: The cove as well, since Eadstan tells a friend of the house what he would not tell a stranger; the scribe as a fast friend; free copying of any text the house holds (copy_text at no cost); the deed won_great_riddle here.

endings.how: You sold the three leaves to the minster at York, which pays better for English verse.
endings.text: York has the riddles and Lindisfarena has a gap. Ceolhelm hears of it from Sigewine within the year.
endings.reward: About 90 d in silver from the archbishop's clerk; the scribe cool, and the writing house shut to this merchant until he brings a gift of skins.

stories.reward: A harbour nobody else has, and either a scribe who will copy anything for the house or York's silver: the choice says who the merchant trades for.

stories.title: The book without a lid
stories.summary: A gospel book lies on the altar in bare boards, its cover of gold and stones torn off for the metal. Ceolhelm will teach a merchant what such a thing is worth, and to whom, if the merchant will carry for the writing house: skins and colours in, and one borrowed book from York.
stories.picture: A large open gospel book on a plain altar cloth, its front board bare wood with nail holes where a jewelled cover was, one lamp, a monk's hand resting on the page.

beats.text: Ceolhelm reckons a book aloud: so many calves, a scribe's year, the gold, and then the price a king's church would pay against the price of the metal on a heathen's scale. The two sums are very far apart. (Sets bk_knows_worth.)
The herdsman has skins but not enough, and no colours at all. The writing house gives a standing order: calfskin, orpiment, red lead, and blue if God sends any. (Sets bk_parchment.)

Alcuin has written telling Higbald to read Gregory's book on the care of souls very often. The island's copy is leaves on a floor. York will lend its own to a merchant the bishop names, against a pledge.
The borrowed book comes over the sand wrapped in two hides. Higbald has it read at table, and Ceolhelm starts the copy the same night.
A book in a heathen house, kept for its pictures, its cover long gone to make a brooch. The merchant alone in that hall knows both prices.

endings.how: You brought York's book to the island and took it back whole when the copy was done.
endings.text: Both houses write the merchant's name in a margin. Sigewine, who was to have carried it, is grateful beyond reason.
endings.reward: The pledge back with 60 d over; the flag bk_carried, which opens book carrying at every minster on the coast; a letter under the bishop's seal that names the house as trusted.

endings.how: You bought a plundered book in the north at the metal's price and brought it to the island.
endings.text: It is not the island's own, but it is a gospel, and it comes home to a church. Ceolhelm finds the house it was made for from the hand, and writes to them.
endings.reward: A third of a book's worth in silver and goods at once (about 120 d) and a second gift when its own house answers; standing with every church that hears of it.

endings.how: The book was in your boat when she filled, or you left it too long in a damp hold.
endings.text: Gregory's book comes ashore as a block of wet skin. York keeps the pledge. Ceolhelm says nothing at all, which is worse.
endings.reward: The pledge is forfeit and bk_lost is set: no minster on this coast trusts the house with a book again until a new one is given. The scribe's price teaching is kept.

stories.reward: The merchant can price a book in any market, has a standing order at the writing house, and holds or loses the trust of the minsters with one cargo.

stories.title: The king of twenty-seven days
stories.summary: In May 796 Osbald, made king after the murder of Æthelred and cast out within the month, comes over the sand with a few men and asks for a ship to the Picts. The brethren will take him in their own boat if they must. A merchant's keel would be faster, and would be remembered at Bebbanburg.
stories.picture: A man in a rich red cloak with mud to the knee stepping into a small boat on a grey beach at dawn, two monks already at the oars, armed riders tiny on the far shore of the sands.

beats.text: A quiet man with a sword-belt mark worn into his tunic and no sword sits by Hunfrith's fire. The cellarer says only that the house has a guest who cannot stay.
Eadstan will take him north in the house's boat with some of the brethren. He says plainly that the merchant's boat is the better sea boat, and that the tide serves for an hour.
King Eardwulf's reeve asks every skipper who was at the island in May who it was that carried Osbald. He asks pleasantly.
Osbald is dead, an abbot, and buried in the minster at York. A clerk there has a small debt of his to settle with whoever helped him to the boat.
The well at York has it first: the king killed at Corbridge, Osbald king, and Osbald out again within the month.

endings.how: You took him north along the coast to the Pictish shore.
endings.text: He pays with an arm ring off his own wrist and says he will pray for the boat. In later years he does; he dies a monk.
endings.reward: A gold-and-silver arm ring worth about 200 d; from 799 a legacy of 60 d paid at York; King Eardwulf's men search the boat hard at Bebbanburg until 806.

endings.how: You stood aside and let the house's own boat take him.
endings.text: The brethren row him out on the ebb. Nobody is angry with the merchant, and nobody is in his debt.
endings.reward: Nothing gained or lost; Hunfrith remembers that the merchant kept his mouth shut, which is worth a welcome.

endings.how: You crossed to Bebbanburg and told the new king's men where he was.
endings.text: Riders reach the sand at the flood and sit their horses on the far shore watching a small boat go north. The bishop learns who sent them.
endings.reward: 30 d and a welcome from the king's reeve at Bebbanburg; Higbald wary, and no sanctuary on the island for this merchant while Higbald lives.

stories.reward: A king's gratitude or a king's suspicion: either way the next king's reeve knows the boat.

stories.title: The saint takes the road
stories.summary: In 875 Halfdan's army winters on the Tyne and Bishop Eardulf decides to go. The body goes on a cart with seven bearers; but a house has more than a body: bread, books, lead, the old and the lame, and the lay folk who cannot walk seven years. The merchant has a keel on the beach.
stories.picture: A cart with a draped coffin crossing wet sand at the ebb under a low winter sun, seven young men walking close about it, a bishop with a staff ahead, and behind them a long straggle of people with bundles.

beats.text: The army's ships lie in the Tyne and its horses are out north of the river. Anyone who sees it knows how far a mounted band rides in two days.
Eardulf listens to what the merchant saw at the Tyne mouth and asks three questions: how many ships, how many horses, how many days. Then he sends for Abbot Eadred.

The coffin goes by the sand; no hand but the bearers' may touch it. Everything else is piled above the weed line: sacks, a chest of books, the leaded head of the old cross, two old brothers on a hurdle. Eardulf asks what the boat will hold and what the merchant wants for it.
The church is locked. A priest and a few households remain; fresh pebbles are still laid on the graves. They ask every boat where the saint is now.
The body rests at Chester-le-Street under King Guthred's peace. The bishop's clerk at York keeps a list of those who helped on the road, and it is not long.
The reeve of the rock offers the saint's people a lay protector for their lands, himself for choice. The bishop answers that the saint has managed without.
The abbot of the mother house, who is sending his own saint's shrine to Ireland, writes what Hi has learned: carry the bones, bury the bell, and do not look behind.

endings.how: You took the stores, the books and the lame across to the mainland and down the coast, and asked nothing.
endings.text: Eardulf writes the merchant's name in the book of the house's friends before the book is packed. It is read with the others wherever the body rests.
endings.reward: From 883, the saint's peace: thirty-seven days' sanctuary at the body for this house and its heirs, and the friendship of Saint Cuthbert's bishop between Tyne and Wear; standing across Northumbria; no silver.

endings.how: You carried them and named a fair freight.
endings.text: The bishop pays in the stycas and Wessex pennies of the alms box, counted out on the shingle, and thanks the merchant civilly.
endings.reward: About 150 d in mixed coin, some of it very base; a welcome from the saint's people, and no more than that.

endings.how: You would not carry, but bought what they could not take: lead, the smith's stock, the cellarer's casks, at a leaving price.
endings.text: It is a good bargain and everyone present knows what kind. The roof plates you did not buy are still on the church in the earl's day.
endings.reward: Lead, iron tools and wine at a third of their worth (a cargo worth about 240 d for 80); the saint's people remember it for a generation.

stories.reward: A place in the book of names and the saint's peace for the heirs, or a cheap cargo: the island does not offer both.

works.name: Doors for Saint Peter's
works.what: Two leaves of oak on iron hinges for the church doorway, which has stood open to the wind and the gulls since the eighth of June, with nails and straps from the smith's shed.
works.needs: Higbald's leave; oak timber brought in, since the island has no trees to speak of.
works.gives: The house's lasting thanks: Higbald and Hunfrith friendly at once, free lodging at the guest house, and the merchant's name said at mass on the day the doors are hung.
works.picture: Two monks and a smith hanging a heavy new oak door on a lead-sheathed church, the old torn hinge still in the post, a merchant holding the door's foot.
works.source: The doors off: the spine's picture of Higbald in 793 (the game's). The oak church: Bede III.25. The smithy: DigVentures 2020.

works.name: Lead to mend the bishop's cross
works.what: The head of Bishop Æthelwold's stone cross, broken off by the heathen, is set back on its shaft and run together with molten lead. The smith needs two pigs of lead and a week of dry weather.
works.needs: Two pigs of lead in the hold or their price; the smith's shed working.
works.gives: The cross stands whole in the graveyard for the rest of the game, and in 875 it goes with the saint. Ceolhelm cuts the giver's name small on the back of the joint (remember, for the heirs).
works.picture: A smith on a ladder pouring bright lead from an iron ladle into the joint of a tall carved stone cross, monks steadying the head with ropes.
works.source: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham xii: the cross's head, broken in 793, was joined with lead, carried about with the body, and stood at Durham in his day. Who paid is not said: the merchant may.

works.name: A watch kept on the Heugh
works.what: Bread, ale and a horn for two laymen to sit on the ridge from the first of May to Michaelmas and look north, so that the brethren can sing the hours without one eye on the sea. It is men and their keep, not a fire: nothing is lit.
works.needs: The bishop's leave, and the payment made again each spring.
works.gives: For that summer the island has warning of ships from the north: word of a band reaches the house and any ship in the Ouse a tide earlier. Eadstan thinks better of the merchant.
works.picture: Two men in rough cloaks sitting against a small stone chapel on a black ridge, one with a horn across his knees, both looking out over an empty northern sea.
works.source: A brother kept watch on a height in 687 (Bede, Life of Cuthbert 40); the tower-like footing on the Heugh (?). No beacon stood here before 1810 (en.wikipedia Lindisfarne): the watch is the game's.

works.name: A name stone for one of yours
works.what: A small slab of sandstone, round-headed, cut with a cross and a name in Roman letters or in runes or both, painted, and set at a grave or kept in the church for one who died at sea.
works.needs: A dead crewman or kinsman to name; the scribe or his successor to draw the letters.
works.gives: The dead of the house are remembered here by name (remember at the graveyard lifts the crew's heart); the stone is still there for the heirs.
works.picture: A hand-sized round-headed stone with an incised cross and a short name in two kinds of letters, fresh red paint in the cuts, lying on turf among white pebbles.
works.source: The Lindisfarne name stones, 7th to 9th century, once painted; one reads Osgyth in runes and in capitals (English Heritage collection; DigVentures 2025). Carved stones continue to the late 10th century.

works.name: A name in the book of the house's friends
works.what: The merchant's name, and his father's, written in the book that lies on the altar and is carried to it at mass: kings and dukes in gold, others in silver, each prayed for by the brethren living and to come.
works.needs: A gift worth the entry (silver, a book, wine for a year) and the bishop's good will: the house does not sell the entry, it answers a gift.
works.gives: Standing with Saint Cuthbert's people that passes whole to the heir, and holds at Chester-le-Street after 883 and at Durham after 995.
works.picture: An open book on an altar, its page ruled in columns of names in alternating gold and silver ink, a quill adding one more at the foot.
works.source: The Durham Liber Vitae, begun about 840, probably at Lindisfarne (en.wikipedia) (?). A merchant's name in it is the game's.

ships.note: A fisher's boat off the Ouse beach, sold when a man dies or the house needs corn more than fish. Good for the Farne rocks and the Tweed mouth, not for the open sea.
ships.picture: A small tarred clinker boat upside down on shingle, a net and a sounding pole laid across her.
ships.source: Boats lay in the Ouse (dossier, section 1); one grave here was made beside boat timbers with clench nails (DigVentures).

ships.note: The house's own boat, which fetches casks from the Tyne and corn from the estates on the Tweed, with Eadstan or his successor in her: hired by the trip when the bishop can spare her. In 875 she is for sale, cheap, to whoever will also carry.
ships.picture: A broad open boat of ten paces with a single square sail of undyed wool, drawn up on a beach below a lead-roofed church, monks loading sacks.
ships.source: Cuthbert's body came by ship in 687; Osbald left by ship with brethren in 796 (Symeon). The house's estates lay on the Tweed and the coast (History of the Kings s.a. 854). That she could be hired is the game's (?).

ships.note: A hide boat from Hi lies on the beach some summers, come round the north with letters from the mother house. Her crew will take a passenger or a small cargo back west for a gift to Columba.
ships.picture: A long hide boat on a wicker frame carried up a beach on the shoulders of four tonsured men, the black rock islet behind.
ships.source: The house was founded from Hi (Bede III.3); the two prayed for each other's dead (spine, cast.bresal). A currach on this beach in the 790s is not recorded (?). Hi's people move to Kells after 806.

sayings.text: Twice a day she makes us an island and twice a day she gives us back.
sayings.source: Said on the island; after Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.3, in our own words

sayings.text: This year the harrowing inroads of heathen men made lamentable havoc in the church of God in Holy-island, by rapine and slaughter.
Some of the brethren they slew, some they carried off with them in chains, the greater number they stripped naked, insulted, and cast out of doors, and some they drowned in the sea.
sayings.source: Symeon of Durham, History of the Church of Durham xx (Stevenson 1855); written three hundred years after

sayings.text: What has Ingeld to do with Christ? The house is narrow; it cannot hold both.
sayings.source: Alcuin, letter of 797 to a bishop once thought to be Higbald (now doubted (?)); our rendering from the Latin (MGH Epistolae IV no. 124)

sayings.text: We owe King Ceolwulf our ale. He gave up a kingdom, and we gave up water.
sayings.source: The cellarer's joke, invented in the period's manner; the fact is Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 854

sayings.text: At need a man must try his friends.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs ('Aet thearfe mann sceal freonda cunnian'), our rendering; written down about 1050 by the saint's own people

sayings.text: Now it is in the pig's judgement, said the churl who sat on the boar's back.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs ('Nu hit ys on swines dome, cwaeth se ceorl saet on eoferes hricge'), our rendering

sayings.text: A moth ate words. It was no wiser for the meal.
sayings.source: After the Exeter Book's bookworm riddle, our own short rendering; the scribe's favourite insult for a careless reader

sayings.text: The wind was wrong for them that day.
sayings.source: What the island says of Bebbanburg and the eighth of June; invented in the period's manner (understatement)
The boatman's word for why a monk should not go in a boat in his habit; invented

easter_eggs.text: The blue glass piece on the guest-house board, with its little crown of white drops, is a king for the game of tafl. Its like is played with at Dorestad and, later, at Dublin. It will be lost in a ditch and found by a digger's trowel in 2019.
easter_eggs.source: DigVentures, the glass gaming king of 700 to 900 (2020)

easter_eggs.text: One stone in the graveyard says the same woman's name twice: OSGYTH in Roman capitals, and again in runes, for readers of either.
easter_eggs.source: English Heritage, Lindisfarne name stones; DigVentures 2025

easter_eggs.text: The white pebbles on the graves are quartz from the shore. Children are sent to gather them. Nobody on the island can say why it is done, only that it always has been.

Six weeks before the heathen men came, the island buried a king-slayer: Sicga, who killed King Ælfwald and died by his own hand, was carried over the sand on 23 April. Some of the brethren have their own opinion of what followed.
easter_eggs.source: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 793

easter_eggs.text: Ask where the name comes from and a brother will walk you down at the lowest ebb to a trickle two feet wide running across the sand: the Lindis, he says. At the flood there is no such stream.
easter_eggs.source: Symeon, History of the Kings s.a. 793; History of the Church of Durham xx

easter_eggs.text: A bone comb in the widow's house has letters scratched on it by someone practising: all that can be read is -EDE.

On the north beach by the cattle steading lie the bones of a bird as tall as a goose that could not fly and swam like a seal. The herdsman's children call it the fat one. There will be none left in the world by 1844.
easter_eggs.source: Great auk bones from the Lindisfarne digs (DigVentures 2024)

easter_eggs.text: A brother who has been to Rome keeps one chip of green stone with white flecks, from an emperor's floor, in a bag round his neck.
easter_eggs.source: A chip of green porphyry found on the island (DigVentures 2024); the brother is invented

easter_eggs.text: The crag at the island's east end is bare rock with gulls on it. There will be no castle there for seven hundred and fifty years.
easter_eggs.source: en.wikipedia Lindisfarne: the castle on Beblowe dates from 1550

easter_eggs.text: After the game's last year: in December 1069 the saint's people will come back to the sand with the body, flying from King William, at full tide at evening. The sea will draw back at that place only and close again at the carriers' heels.
easter_eggs.source: Symeon, History of the Church of Durham l (Stevenson 1855)

easter_eggs.text: Between the lines of the great gospel book a priest named Aldred will one day write the English for every Latin word, and add a note saying who wrote the book, who bound it and who covered it. He is not born yet.
easter_eggs.source: en.wikipedia Lindisfarne Gospels: Aldred's gloss and colophon, about 950 to 970 (?)

unlocks.what: The bishop's list: the names of the boys and what the house will pay
unlocks.how: Speak with Higbald at the church before his death in May 803, or be given the list by Sigewine at Quentovic.
unlocks.gives: flag lf_knows_boys; give_text alcuin_793 if the chest lacks it; northern dealers can now be asked about the boys by name.

unlocks.what: The bed nearest the fire in the guest house
unlocks.how: Bring the house bread corn in the famine of 793, or wine or wax in any year, twice running as promised.
unlocks.gives: Free lodging (lodge) and stores at cost (provision) on the island; Hunfrith's news before the guest fire's (ask_news); passes to the heir at half strength, as feeling does.

unlocks.what: Eadstan's marks for the sand and the Ouse
unlocks.how: Hire him as pilot three times, or help him with the boat on the day of the king of twenty-seven days.
unlocks.gives: The house's ships enter and leave the Ouse at any state of the tide without a pilot, and cross to Bebbanburg in fog; hire_pilot here costs nothing.

unlocks.what: The scribe's reckoning of a book
unlocks.how: Sit through Ceolhelm's sum in the writing house and take his order for skins.
unlocks.gives: flag bk_knows_worth and flag bk_parchment: books can be priced in a heathen market, and calfskin and pigments sell here at a fifth over the market.

unlocks.what: A copy of the first storm leaf
unlocks.how: Pay Ceolhelm ten pennies in the writing house, any year before 876.
unlocks.gives: give_riddle riddle_exeter_01_storm_land; with the leaves of Gyrwe and Streonaeshalch, the landing among the Farne islands (rw_cove_farne).

unlocks.what: The peace of Saint Cuthbert for the house
unlocks.how: Carry for the saint's people in 875 and ask nothing, or have the house's name written in the book of friends between 840 and 875.
unlocks.gives: From 883, sanctuary for thirty-seven days at the saint's body for the merchant and his heirs, and the good word of the saint's bishop between Tyne and Wear.

unlocks.what: The names read on the eighth of June
unlocks.how: Follow the bishop's count to any of its ends.
unlocks.gives: Each year the house lies at the island on that day, the crew hears the names of the boys read, and the merchant's among the helpers if he earned it (morale; remember).
